question: A team has revised its Claude-assisted reporting arrangement four times in two months. The latest version is worse for certain reports, and nobody can work out which change caused it. What practice would have helped most?
options: A) Testing each revision on a larger sample of reports before it replaced the earlier version.
B) Having a single person own all revisions so the changes are made consistently over time.
C) Limiting revisions to one per month so that each change has time to settle before the next.
D) Recording what changed at each revision and why, so a step backwards can be traced.
correct_answers: D) Recording what changed at each revision and why, so a step backwards can be traced.
explanations: Wider testing would have caught the regression sooner, which is valuable. It still would not tell the team which change was responsible, so they could not undo the right one.
A single owner makes changes more consistent and is good practice. It does not help anyone reconstruct which of four revisions introduced the regression once the memory of them has faded.

Slowing the pace of change reduces how often revisions collide, but four undocumented changes over eight months would leave the team in the same position. The problem is that nothing was recorded, not that it happened quickly.

Correct. Iteration only compounds if each change is traceable. A short record of what was altered and why lets the team match the regression to the revision that caused it and roll back precisely instead of guessing.
